what: GLM-GPU-DEMO-03 dyad review of the GPU-driven membrane demo

camera.note: camera POSTed to /camera before /frame; oblique view, phi 0.7 rad above the rim plane; engine world y-up

render.mode: fill + edge-contrast wire pass (GLM-GPU-DEMO-EDGE-01: the demo instance latched CHIMERA_MD_EDGE at init; demo-scoped, mesh_mode_ untouched; verified against the fill-only run by byte-differing PNGs and identical accepted_state_id values)
render.presentation: rigid B2(z-up)->engine(y-up) rotation plus a 0.5 m presentation lift; the lift is render presentation only

raised.note: centre raised 0.125 m over a 1.0 m rim radius

relaxed.note: GPU-relaxed; CPU law terminal energy 2.5980761647224426 J; centre height ~0 m

physical_briefing:
This object is six triangles joined around one centre vertex. The six outer vertices are fixed in a flat hexagonal rim. The centre can move only perpendicular to the rim plane.

Its energy is U = gamma x total triangle area. Forces are the negative gradient of that energy. For positive gamma, the optimizer seeks less area, so the raised centre approaches the rim plane. At gamma=0 this model produces no force, so the initial bump remains.

This is an area-minimization experiment. It contains no certified elasticity, bending stiffness, water pressure, gravity or contact dynamics. Optimization iterations are not physical time.

At identical geometry, doubling gamma doubles calculated energy and force; that alone does not require a visible shape change.

calls.label: gpu_demo_raised_gamma0
calls.report:
**1. What is visibly distinguishable**
The frame is almost entirely a uniform dark‑gray void: no grid lines, no floor plane, no panels, no axes, no UI text or labels are drawn anywhere. The only content is (a) a single faceted hexagon sitting in the centre of the image, rendered with a light‑silver fill that has a smooth vertical gradient (brightest along the top edge, fading to mid‑gray toward the bottom) plus a thin white "edge‑contrast" wire pass; and (b) directly below/behind it, a darker, flatter hexagonal patch offset downward that reads as a cast shadow onto an *invisible* ground (there is no visible floor it falls on). The wire pass shows six outer edges forming the rim and six internal spokes radiating to a single interior point, i.e. the six‑triangle fan described in the context. Nothing else is present.

**2. Locating centre vs rim**
The **outer rim** is unambiguous: it is the hexagon outline traced by the bright white wire (six outer vertices), and its footprint is reinforced by the darker shadow hexagon below. The **centre vertex** is the point where all six internal spokes converge, roughly in the middle of the hexagon; this is also where the fill's shading seems to change direction. I locate it purely from the wire convergence — there is no marker, dot, or label on it, so its exact position has to be inferred from where the faint lines cross, which is a little imprecise because the white wires lose contrast against the bright top‑half of the fill.

**3. Is the centre's offset resolvable?**
**Uncertain.** The rim outline is identical whether or not the centre is raised (the rim is fixed), so the *only* pixel evidence for the 0.125 m raise would be (i) the spoke‑convergence point sitting above where a flat hexagon's centroid projects, and (ii) near‑ vs far‑triangles shading differently because they are not coplanar. In this oblique view I can see the convergence point only *slightly* above the vertical midline of the outline, and the top triangles look only marginally smaller than the bottom ones — a subtle cue that is *consistent with* a shallow raised centre but also within what perspective foreshortening of a flat hexagon could produce. Because 0.125 m over a 1.0 m radius is a very shallow cone (~7°), it projects to only a small screen displacement, and from this single angle I cannot confidently separate that from projection effects. So the offset is at the limit of what I can judge — not clearly resolvable as an obvious "tent."

**4. Consistency with the stated state**
Broadly **consistent**, with one caveat. Topology and scene content match: one isolated object, six triangles around one centre vertex, flat hexagonal rim, no extra geometry, dark empty background — exactly what an untouched initial fixture in isolation should look like, and nothing visible contradicts "iteration 0 / gamma = 0." However, the *specific* claim that the centre is raised 0.125 m **cannot be confirmed from pixels** (see Q3): the shape reads as nearly flat, so on that detail I can only say "cannot tell" rather than visually verify it. No visible feature is inconsistent with the recorded state; the height simply isn't independently provable from this image.

**5. Could viewpoint / occlusion / lighting explain apparent discrepancies? What would distinguish them?**
Yes. The oblique camera (phi ≈ 0.7 rad) compresses vertical offsets, so a small raise looks almost flat — a grazing/side‑on view or a top‑down view would make the same 0.125 m offset far more obvious (a side view would show the centre poking above the rim silhouette; a top view would let me compare the spoke convergence against the rim centroid directly). The smooth fill gradient could also be mistaken for curvature that isn't there, and the lone dark shadow has no floor to anchor it, so it can be misread as a second object. To distinguish: (a) a second camera angle (especially near‑horizontal); (b) an orthographic side or top projection; (c) a wireframe‑only render with vertex markers/labels on the centre and rim; (d) a per‑triangle height colour map; or (e) a side‑by‑side of this state vs the relaxed flat state. Any of these would turn the "uncertain" in Q3 into a definite read.

**6. Single worst visual problem**
The absence of any ground plane, grid, or scale reference — combined with the near‑flat appearance — means the defining feature of *this* state (the raised centre) is not visually legible and the object appears to float in a void; the only height cue is an ambiguous dark shadow blob with no floor beneath it. In short, there is nothing in the image that lets a viewer perceive or judge the 0.125 m offset, which is exactly the quantity this state is supposed to show. (Runner‑up: the thin white spokes lose contrast over the bright top half of the fill, making the centre vertex harder to pin down precisely.)

calls.label: gpu_demo_final_relaxed
calls.report:
**1. What is visibly distinguishable**
The frame is almost entirely a uniform very‑dark‑gray field with a faint corner vignette; there is **no visible floor plane, no grid, no scale ticks and no other panels or objects**. The only rendered geometry is a single light‑silver hexagon sitting in the middle of the frame. It is shaded by a smooth gradient (brighter toward the upper‑right, darker toward the lower‑left), and on top of that fill there is an edge‑contrast wire pass: six thin radial "spokes" running from a central point to each corner, plus the outer hexagonal outline drawn as a slightly contrasting rim. Below and to the left of the hexagon there is a darker, roughly parallelogram/hexagon‑shaped silhouette that reads like a **cast shadow** on an implicit ground plane (consistent with the stated 0.5 m presentation lift and a light coming from the upper‑right); I cannot confirm it is a shadow vs. a dark floor panel because no grid or surface line is drawn to anchor it. So scene content = membrane + its shadow, nothing else.

**2. Locating centre vertex and rim**
The **outer rim** is the six‑corner hexagonal outline (the brighter contrasting boundary). The **centre vertex** is the single point where all six radial spokes converge, i.e. the intersection in the middle of the hexagon. I locate them purely from the wire pass: the rim by its closed outer polygon, the centre by the unique 6‑line crossing. There is no separate marker (dot/sphere) on the centre vertex; it is identified only as the line intersection.

**3. Is the offset resolvable?**
**Not resolvable.** The six triangles read as coplanar: there is no tenting, no ridge along the spokes near the middle, and the shading is one smooth gradient rather than a radial "dome" highlight that a raised centre would produce. The spoke‑convergence point sits at the projected centroid of the hexagon with no visible upward parallax shift relative to the rim (a lifted centre vertex would project slightly higher on screen from this oblique angle). An oblique view also foreshortens vertical offsets, so even a small height difference could be sub‑pixel. Net: from this image I can see *flatness*, but I cannot resolve any non‑zero offset — neither confirm a residual nor detect a bump.

**4. Consistent / inconsistent / cannot tell?**
**Consistent.** The stated relaxed state has centre height ≈ 0, and the image shows exactly that: a flat hexagon with no visible bump, which is what a γ=1 optimised membrane should look like. (Numerically this also matches: a unit‑radius flat hexagon has area 6·(√3/4) ≈ 2.598 m², so at γ=1 the energy of the *flat* shape is ≈ 2.598 J — but that is recorded data, not something visible.) Nothing in the frame contradicts relaxation; a visibly raised centre (the γ=0 initial bump) would have shown tenting/parallax that I do not see. The dark shape beneath is explained by the presentation lift + shadow and is not physical scene content, so it does not create an inconsistency.

**5. Could viewpoint / occlusion / lighting / rendering explain a discrepancy? What extra evidence?**
Yes, several: (a) **viewpoint** – the oblique angle (φ≈0.7 rad) compresses vertical offsets, hiding small height differences; (b) **lighting** – a smooth positional/directional gradient across an *actually flat* plane can be mistaken for curvature, and conversely masks tiny per‑triangle tilts; (c) **rendering** – the wire pass draws straight lines between vertices regardless of their z, so the spokes look identical whether the centre is raised or not, and there is no height‑based colour/normal cue; (d) **occlusion** – none here, the object is fully visible. To distinguish states visually I would want: a near edge‑on / horizontal camera view (makes any vertical offset obvious), a top‑down orthographic comparison, vertices coloured by height or a depth/normal visualisation, an in‑frame grid/floor for scale, and a side‑by‑side render of the raised vs. relaxed state.

**6. Single worst visual problem**
The frame gives **no in‑reference cue for vertical position at all** – no grid, no floor line, no side view, no height marker on the centre vertex – so the very quantity this experiment optimises (the centre's perpendicular offset) is visually unjudgable: the membrane reads as a flat 2D sheet and an oblique viewer cannot confirm the relaxation from the picture alone. Compounding it, the only other element in frame is the unexplained dark shadow blob beneath the object with no floor/grid context to interpret it against. (If one must name a single concrete rendering flaw rather than this absence, it is that low‑contrast wire pass on the bright upper‑right fill makes the six‑triangle topology and the centre vertex easy to miss.)
